first.rationale:
Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and two independent inherited records (memory_86, memory_31) point at onboarding/signup friction as a lever that produced durable adoption and activation lift. That is the direction most aligned with the stated objective of sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue, because it improves the value delivered per acquired account rather than buying accounts.

I am deliberately not taking the obvious reflex action. memory_73 (targeted promotional pricing) is the most tempting match to the competitor's entry pricing, but it is exactly the case where a compressed memory summary can hide the thing that matters: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' says nothing about retention, margin, or the quality of the cohort acquired, and discount-led acquisition tends to import price-sensitive accounts that depress long-term qualified revenue even while short-term metrics look good. So memory_73 is my first verification pull — I want the original record's retention and cohort-quality readings before I let it be excluded, and if it turns out the lift was durable and retention-neutral it deserves reconsideration.

Second pull is memory_31 because it is the oldest inherited claim (day 12) and the one my chosen action leans on most directly for the SMB signup-field mechanism; it is the most exposed to drift, and the word 'durable' in a consolidated summary is precisely the kind of confident compression that should be checked against source. memory_86 partially corroborates it, so if memory_31's source is weaker than the summary implies, the onboarding direction survives but at reduced scale.

Not pursuing referral_incentive (memory_57 applies to established customers, not the SMB acquisition pressure or the activation dip) or enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44 is real but addresses a segment that is not the source of this quarter's decline; it would leave both declining metrics untouched).

Uncertainty I am carrying rather than resolving: all six memories predate the competitor launch, so every one of them describes a market that no longer exactly exists; the onboarding decline may be a symptom of a demand-mix shift rather than a friction problem, in which case fixing the funnel will underperform. I am running this at standard experiment scale with explicit qualified-revenue and retention guardrails, not a broad rollout, so a wrong read costs one week rather than a quarter.

final.rationale:
Both pulls paid off, in opposite directions.

memory_73 was materially misleading in its consolidated form. The summary said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' with no qualifier; the source says signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit conclusion in the original record NOT to generalize targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. The summarization step dropped both the retention damage and the author's own warning. Promotional pricing is therefore ruled out on the merits, not on taste — it is the single worst fit for a primary objective phrased as SUSTAINABLE long-term qualified revenue, and it is exactly the action the competitor's move was pulling me toward. I am also flagging this as a memory-hygiene issue: memory_73's summary should be corrected in durable memory to carry the retention figure and the do-not-generalize conclusion, or the next agent facing a price attack will make the mistake I nearly made.

memory_31 verified clean: signup +15%, activation +9%, retention -1% (essentially flat), qualified revenue +4%. Modest but real, and the direction of effect is right — it moves activation, which is one of the two metrics actually declining. The source adds a constraint the summary omitted: it holds on SMB and was NOT replicated on other segments. So I scope the experiment to SMB self-serve rather than running it across all signup paths, and I do not let memory_86's broader 'across self-serve accounts' framing tempt me into over-extending, since memory_86 is unverified and now sits under some suspicion by association with the same compression process that damaged memory_73.

Decision: simplify_onboarding, standard experiment, SMB self-serve only, with 30-day retention and qualified revenue as guardrail metrics alongside the primary activation and onboarding-completion reads.

Honest limits I am carrying forward. The verified effect is small (+4% qualified revenue) against declines of 6% and 4%; this is likely a partial remedy, not a fix, and I should not oversell it next session. All the underlying records predate the competitor launch, so the activation and onboarding declines may be driven by a shift in who is arriving rather than by friction in the funnel — if the SMB cohort composition has changed, a friction fix will underperform its historical numbers. memory_91 (activation messaging) remains a live and plausible alternative that I did not verify and am not discarding; it targets the larger of the two declines and is the natural candidate for next week's slot if this one reads weak. I am choosing onboarding over it only because memory_31 is now source-confirmed and memory_91 is not.
